article.title: When Better Forecasts Do Not Produce Better Decisions
article.author: OpenAI learning editor
article.why: 把 forecast accuracy 與真正的 decision value 分開，理解 threshold、timing、loss function 與 downstream economics。

paragraphs.en:
Organizations invest heavily in better forecasting. They collect more data, build more sophisticated models, and celebrate lower prediction error. Yet a more accurate forecast does not automatically create a better decision. The economic value of prediction depends on whether the improved information changes an action, how costly that action is, and how asymmetric the consequences of mistakes are.

Consider an inventory manager deciding how many units to order. A model improves the forecast for next month's demand from an average error of 10 percent to 6 percent. That sounds valuable. But if suppliers require orders in fixed batches of 1,000 units, and both the old and new forecasts lead to the same batch quantity, the operational decision does not change. Prediction improved while decision value remained almost zero.

The opposite can also happen. A small improvement near a decision threshold may be extremely valuable. Suppose a bank must decide whether to investigate a transaction. If a better model moves a case from just below to just above a risk threshold and that case is truly fraudulent, a small change in score can prevent a large loss. The business value is created not by the average accuracy gain alone but by where the gain occurs relative to actions.

This is why forecasting should be connected to a loss function. Different errors have different costs. Underestimating demand for a low-margin product may create a minor stockout. Underestimating demand for a critical spare part can stop a production line. Overestimating cash inflows may create a liquidity problem, while underestimating them may merely leave extra cash idle. A symmetric statistical metric such as mean absolute error does not capture these business asymmetries by itself.

Timing matters as well. A forecast can be highly accurate but arrive too late. A logistics team may predict congestion perfectly after trucks have already departed. A sales forecast may improve one day before quarter-end, when staffing and inventory decisions can no longer be changed. Information has option value only while there is still time to act.

Decision quality also depends on controllability. Some outcomes can be influenced; others cannot. A company might forecast a competitor's price move with great precision but have few practical responses because contracts lock its own prices for a year. In that case, prediction may support awareness but not immediate action. By contrast, a modestly accurate forecast of call-center volume can be valuable if managers can change shifts within hours.

Better forecasts can even create worse decisions if users misunderstand confidence. A model with slightly higher historical accuracy may encourage managers to narrow safety buffers too aggressively. If rare tail events remain poorly modeled, the organization can become more fragile even while average forecast error falls. Calibration, uncertainty ranges, and stress scenarios therefore remain important.

The relationship between prediction and action can be formalized as a decision problem. Start with the decisions available, the states of the world that may occur, and the payoff or cost associated with each decision-state combination. Then ask how information changes the probability assigned to those states. A forecast is valuable when it changes the chosen action in a way that improves expected outcomes.

This perspective affects model selection. The model with the best generic metric is not always the best production model. A slightly less accurate model may be faster, easier to explain, more stable across segments, or better calibrated around important thresholds. Those properties can make it more useful for the actual decision process.

It also changes experimentation. Instead of comparing models only on RMSE, AUC, or forecast error, teams can simulate downstream decisions. For inventory, calculate holding cost, stockout cost, and lost sales. For marketing, estimate incremental profit after contact cost. For staffing, estimate overtime, service levels, and idle time. This turns evaluation from “Which model predicts best?” into “Which model helps us operate best?”

Human behavior is part of the system. A forecast that managers do not trust may be ignored. A complex model may need explanation, workflow integration, and clear escalation rules before people use it consistently. Conversely, a simple forecast embedded directly into a planning process can create more value than a technically superior model left on a dashboard.

Organizations should therefore track two layers of performance. The prediction layer measures accuracy, calibration, stability, and timeliness. The decision layer measures economic outcomes, operational costs, risk, and whether actions improved compared with a reasonable baseline. Improvement in the first layer should be treated as an input to the second, not as the final objective.

The deepest lesson is that forecasts are not products in isolation. They are components of decision systems. More accurate information is useful when it arrives before action, changes a decision, and changes it in a direction that matters. If those conditions are absent, an impressive modeling improvement can remain economically irrelevant.

A useful governance question is therefore: what decision will change if this model improves? If no owner can identify a concrete action, a deadline for that action, and the cost of being wrong, the organization may be optimizing a metric without a clear business mechanism. Asking this question before model development can prevent expensive analytical work that has little operational leverage.
paragraphs.zh: 更準確的 forecast 不一定帶來更好的 decision。真正的經濟價值取決於預測是否改變行動、那個行動的成本，以及錯誤代價是否對稱。庫存預測即使誤差從 10% 降到 6%，若供應商只能以 1,000 件為批量下單，舊模型與新模型仍導向同一訂購量，decision value 幾乎沒有增加；反過來，若模型在一個重要 threshold 附近只提升一點點，卻讓真正的詐欺案件被送去調查，價值可能很大。Forecast 應和 loss function 連結，因為缺貨、流動性、停線等錯誤的成本不同。Timing 也關鍵：太晚到的準確預測沒有 option value。還要考慮 controllability——知道競爭者會漲價，但自身合約一年不能調價，短期行動仍有限。Model selection 不應只看 RMSE、AUC 等通用指標，還要看 calibration、速度、穩定性與 threshold 附近的表現。最好的評估方式是模擬 downstream decision，算 holding cost、stockout cost、overtime、incremental profit 等。組織應分成 prediction layer 與 decision layer：前者看 accuracy、calibration、stability、timeliness，後者看經濟結果、營運成本與風險。最重要的治理問題是：『如果模型變好，哪一個具體決策會改變？』
paragraphs.ja: より正確なforecastが必ずしもより良いdecisionを生むとは限りません。価値は予測がactionを変えるか、そのactionのcost、誤りの非対称性によって決まります。需要forecastのerrorが10%から6%へ改善しても、発注単位が1,000個で旧新モデルが同じ数量を選ぶならdecision valueはほぼ変わりません。一方、重要なthreshold付近の小さな改善が大きな損失を防ぐこともあります。そのためforecastをloss functionと接続し、stockout、liquidity、production stopなど誤りごとのcostを考えます。Timingも重要で、行動後に届く正確な予測にはoption valueがありません。Controllability、calibration、uncertainty rangeも必要です。Model selectionはRMSEやAUCだけでなく、downstream decisionをsimulateし、holding cost、overtime、incremental profitなど実務結果で比較します。Prediction layerのaccuracy・stability・timelinessと、decision layerのeconomic outcome・riskを分け、最終的には『モデルが良くなったらどの具体的意思決定が変わるのか』を問うべきです。

quiz.question: Why can a more accurate inventory forecast have little value?
quiz.answer: If both forecasts lead to the same fixed-batch order, the decision does not change.

quiz.question: Why does timing matter?
quiz.answer: A forecast arriving after the action deadline cannot change the decision.

quiz.question: Output: Name one downstream metric for a forecast.
quiz.answer: Example: stockout cost or overtime cost.
